lesson.subtitle: Lesson 1 -- Thirty Seconds on a Call
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Flávio Masaharu Kuroda | Lesson 1 -- Thirty Seconds on a Call

listenings.text: I stopped opening a first call with a sentence about the platform a long time ago. Nobody on the other side wants the technology in the first minute, and honestly they are not listening yet. So I open with their Monday morning instead. I say: somewhere in your company there is a person who spends Monday looking for an invoice that three different systems disagree about. That is the sentence that makes people put down their phone. Then I tell them who we sell to. Mid-market companies, always. Big enough to have a real problem, small enough that one person still knows everybody's name. And then, because a partner always wants to know what is moving right now and not only what we always do, I tell them what the team is working on this quarter. At the moment we are rolling out a new integration, and we are giving it to a small group of customers first, before anybody else touches it.

I take about six of these calls a week, and I will be honest with you: the decision is usually made in the first ten minutes. Not because I am in a hurry, but because the first ten minutes tell me everything. The vendors I call back describe a customer I recognise. They say something like, four people are handling thousands of invoices a month and nobody can close the month on time, and I think, yes, I know that company, I have three of them. The ones I do not call back describe a product. Beautiful architecture, very complete, fully configurable, and after five minutes I still cannot picture who is using it or why. One more thing, because people ask me this and they are usually embarrassed to. English that is not perfect has never been the reason I said no. Not once. What loses the call is a long answer with no customer in it.
